methodological_rigor.justification: This is a secondary qualitative content analysis of three open-ended survey questions from the 2016 Canadian Transitions Survey, restricted to 399 respondents aged 85+ who disclosed income and sex. Inductive coding by two investigators with team consensus is described and is appropriate for content analysis, but inter-rater reliability is not quantified (no kappa) and no theoretical saturation criterion is reported. The analysis relies on brief, often incomplete written responses (authors acknowledge), and very high non-response rates (59.6% blank for challenges, 86% no suggestions) raise substantial selection bias concerns that are acknowledged but not statistically addressed. Chi-square tests on frequencies across four subgroups are used without multiplicity correction, and many cell counts are small.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Findings surface concerns of the oldest-old cancer survivors in Canada (physical limitations, emotional distress, communication gaps) and suggest integration of geriatric assessment and nurse-led support services — plausible but broad, and largely consistent with existing literature. Useful for program planning and hypothesis generation but not directly practice-changing. Classified Oxford LoE 4 as secondary analysis of a cross-sectional mailed survey with no comparison group or outcomes.

reporting_quality.justification: No specific reporting standard is cited; qualitative content analysis would typically invoke COREQ or SRQR, neither of which is referenced (standard_used = 'other'). Core items (sample derivation, coding process, investigator roles, ethics approvals) are present, but other items (researcher reflexivity, audit trail, use of software, direct quote provenance beyond sex, coding tree) are underreported. Positive: the parent dataset is stated to be publicly available via the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer, supporting a data-availability score of 3, but no code or coding manual is shared.

novelty_literature.justification: The study is the 'first in Canada' to examine gender-by-income intersections in cancer survivors aged 85+ per the authors, but the major themes (physical decline, emotional distress, communication gaps, need for geriatric assessment) are extensively documented in prior work including the authors' own prior Transitions-Survey publications (refs 15, 51, 52). Findings are incremental, largely confirmatory, and explicitly framed by the authors as hypothesis-generating. Novelty is limited by substantial overlap with prior analyses of the same parent dataset.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized and clearly written, with thoughtful Discussion situating findings within Canadian demographic and policy context. Illustrative quotes are effective, and limitations and implications are transparently laid out. Minor issues include some redundancy in Discussion/Implications sections and typos in the reference list, but overall presentation is strong.

key_strengths: Focuses on a rarely studied but clinically important population (cancer survivors aged 85+) across all Canadian provinces
Transparent description of coding process, consensus meetings, and parent-study provenance
Thoughtful reflection on very high non-response rates and their interpretive implications
Practical implications linked to geriatric assessment and nurse-led survivorship care
key_concerns: Very brief open-ended responses limit depth of qualitative inference; authors concede interview-based follow-up is needed
No formal qualitative reporting standard (e.g., COREQ or SRQR) invoked; inter-rater reliability not quantified
High non-response (59.6% blank for challenges; 86% no suggestions) introduces substantial selection bias
Chi-square tests applied to small cell counts across four subgroups without multiplicity adjustment
Findings largely confirm earlier publications drawing on the same Transitions Survey, limiting incremental novelty
Heteronormative binary framework limits generalizability; authors acknowledge
chief_reviewer.rationale: Competent but incremental secondary analysis of a national survey; suitable for a tier-3 supportive-care or geriatric-oncology journal after major revisions to address reporting standards, reliability metrics, and framing relative to prior publications by the same team.
